chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar from Safwan from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj who said:
A child was born to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) in Mina, so he sent to us on the Day of Sacrifice (Eid al-Adha) khabeez (sweet flatbread) with saffron, and we had already shaved (our heads).
Abd al-Rahman said: So I ate, but al-Kahili and Murazm refrained from eating it, and they said: 'We have not yet visited the Kaaba (performed Umrah/Hajj rites).'
So Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) heard our words and said to Musadif, who was the messenger who brought it to us, 'What were they talking about?'
He said: 'Abd al-Rahman ate, and the other two refused, saying: We have not yet visited the Kaaba.'
He said: 'Abd al-Rahman was correct.' Then he said: 'Do you not remember when it was brought to us on a day like this, and I ate from it, and my brother Abd Allah refused to eat from it?'
So when my father came, he urged him against me, and he said: 'O my father, indeed Musa ate khabeez with saffron and had not yet visited (the Kaaba).'
So my father (peace be upon him) said: 'He is more learned in jurisprudence than you. Have you not shaved your heads?'

key_terms.إِبَاحَةُ الْأَكْلِ: The permissibility of eating (in the context of Ihram/Hajj)
key_terms.حَلَقْنَا: We shaved (our heads, indicating exit from Ihram)
key_terms.خَبِيصٌ: A type of sweet flatbread or cake

ai.seo_question: Does eating food invalidate Ihram or Hajj rituals according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the scholarly debate among companions regarding the permissibility of eating during Ihram before the final Tawaf, specifically contrasting the cautious stance of Al-Kahili and Murazim with the practice of Abdullah ibn al-Hanafiyya. Imam al-Hasan (AS) validates the latter by referencing the precedent of Prophet Musa (AS), emphasizing that the shaving of the head (Halq) signifies the completion of the core Hajj rites, thereby allowing consumption of food even if the Kaaba visit is pending. This narrative underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that major acts of worship, once completed, permit the resumption of normal activities like eating, distinguishing between ritual purity and physical sustenance.
